items.prompt: What does the "CI" in CI/CD stand for?

options.label: Central Infrastructure
Continuous Integration
Continuous Inspection
Code Isolation

rubric: CI is Continuous Integration: merging and verifying changes frequently.
Other options are plausible-sounding but are not standard terms.

items.prompt: Which pipeline stage turns source code into a deployable package such as a JAR or container image?

options.label: Rollback
Monitoring
Build
Code review

rubric: The build stage compiles and packages code into an artifact.
Rollback and monitoring happen around release, not packaging.

items.prompt: What is a pipeline trigger?

options.label: A test that fails on purpose to check alerts
A server setting that limits how many jobs run
An event, such as a push or pull request, that starts a run
A script that deletes old build artifacts

rubric: A trigger is the event that starts a pipeline run.
Distractors describe unrelated pipeline features.

items.prompt: Where should a pipeline's deployment password or API key be stored?

options.label: In a committed `.env` file in the repo
In the CI tool's secrets store
In the project README for the team
In the pipeline YAML as plain text

rubric: Secrets belong in the CI tool's encrypted secrets store.
The other options expose the secret in the repository.

items.prompt: In which directory does GitHub Actions look for workflow definition files?

options.label: ci/pipelines/
.actions/jobs/
workflows/.github/
.github/workflows/

rubric: Workflows live in `.github/workflows/` as YAML files.
Other paths are invented lookalikes.

items.prompt: Which of these are typical stages in a CI/CD pipeline? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rewrite the Git history
Run automated tests
Build the code
Deploy to an environment
Hire code reviewers

rubric: Build, test and deploy are standard pipeline stages.
Rewriting history and hiring are not pipeline stages.

items.prompt: A team's pipeline has three stages in order: build, test, deploy. A developer pushes a commit and one unit test fails in the test stage. By default, what happens to the deploy stage?

options.label: It is skipped because the pipeline stops at the failed stage
It runs but only on a staging server
It runs anyway and flags the failure later
It waits until the developer fixes the test

rubric: By default, a failed stage stops later stages from running.
Distractors assume the pipeline continues or pauses.

items.prompt: Why do teams run automated tests on every commit rather than once a week?

options.label: It removes the need for code review
It lets developers skip testing locally
It catches integration problems while the change is small
It makes the build artifact smaller

rubric: Frequent runs surface problems early, when they are easy to trace.
Distractors claim unrelated or false benefits.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

options.label: Delivery needs a manual approval before production; deployment releases automatically
Delivery skips the tests that deployment runs
Deployment only builds artifacts; delivery releases them
Delivery targets mobile apps; deployment targets web apps

rubric: Delivery keeps a manual release gate; deployment automates it.
Other options confuse the stages or the platforms.

items.prompt: A pipeline is configured to build and test on every push, but deploy only on the `main` branch. What happens when a developer pushes to branch `feature-x`?

options.label: Only the deploy stage runs
Build, test and deploy all run
Build and test run, but deploy is skipped
Nothing runs until the branch is merged

rubric: Branch conditions skip deploy while build and test still run.
Other options misread the trigger and condition rules.

items.prompt: Why do teams build an artifact once and promote that same artifact through test, staging and production?

options.label: Rebuilding is not allowed by CI tools
Environments cannot run source code
Artifacts become smaller each time they move
The tested binary is exactly what ships to production

rubric: Promoting one artifact ensures what was tested is what is released.
Distractors give false technical limits.

items.prompt: What does a rollback accomplish in a deployment pipeline?

options.label: It rebuilds the code with extra logging enabled
It rewrites Git history to remove the bad commit
It deletes the failing tests from the repo
It redeploys a previous known-good version to restore service

rubric: Rollback restores the last good release quickly.
Other options describe changes to code or history, not release recovery.

items.prompt: Which practices help keep pipeline secrets safe? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rotate a secret right after it leaks
Give every job access to every secret
Limit each secret to the jobs that need it
Print them in logs when debugging a failed job
Store them in the CI secrets store, not in code

rubric: Secure storage, rotation and least access reduce exposure.
Logging or broadly sharing secrets increases leak risk.

items.prompt: A team's pipeline builds, tests and, when all tests pass on `main`, releases straight to production with no human approval. A new developer asks what this practice is called.

options.label: Continuous integration only
Blue-green testing
Continuous delivery with manual release
Continuous deployment

rubric: Automatic release to production after passing tests is continuous deployment.
Delivery would include a manual approval step; CI alone stops at testing.

items.prompt: What is the key difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

options.label: Delivery needs no pipeline, while deployment requires a pipeline to move code between environments
Delivery only builds artifacts, while deployment is the only practice that runs automated tests
Delivery releases to production on every commit, while deployment is limited to staging environments
Delivery keeps a manual approval before production, while deployment releases every passing change automatically

rubric: Continuous delivery keeps code releasable with a human gate; continuous deployment removes that gate.
Distractors swap the terms or claim that one practice skips testing or pipelines.

items.prompt: Why do many pipelines build an artifact once and promote that same artifact through test, staging and production?

options.label: It makes the build run faster because production never needs any compiled files
It lets each environment use its own source branch, so the code can differ safely
It guarantees that what was tested is exactly what ships, instead of a fresh rebuild that might differ
It removes the need for tests in staging because the artifact was already built

rubric: Promoting one artifact avoids differences between rebuilds, so test results apply to what is deployed.
Distractors confuse speed or skipping tests with the real reason: consistency.

items.prompt: Why should an API key be stored in the CI system's secret store rather than committed in the repository?

options.label: Secrets in the repository are fine for private repos, as long as the key is renamed regularly
The secret store makes the key work faster, because stored values are cached on agents
Repository history is widely readable and permanent, so a committed key stays exposed even if later deleted
Committed files cannot be read by pipeline jobs, so the key would never be found

rubric: Git history keeps deleted secrets and many people can read it, so the key can leak.
Distractors claim technical impossibility, speed gains or that private repos make it safe.

items.prompt: A pipeline runs fast unit tests first and slow end-to-end tests afterwards. What is the main reason for this order?

options.label: Running slow tests last guarantees that they always pass because the code was already checked
Quick checks fail early and give feedback sooner, so slow tests don't waste time on broken code
End-to-end tests cannot run until all unit tests have been deleted from the project
Unit tests are always more important, so the slow tests can be ignored if they fail

rubric: Failing fast gives quick feedback and saves compute on obviously broken changes.
Distractors invent dependencies or treat slower tests as optional.

items.prompt: In a typical pipeline with separate test and deploy stages, the test stage fails. What normally happens to the deploy stage?

options.label: It is skipped, because later stages only run when earlier required stages succeed
It runs anyway, because deploy stages are independent of test results by default
It runs after the test stage is retried automatically until it finally passes
It runs but only to a staging environment, because the failure is downgraded to a warning

rubric: Stages run in sequence and a failure stops the later ones by default.
Distractors assume independence, automatic downgrade or infinite retry.

items.prompt: Which of the following are benefits of running a CI pipeline on every pull request? Select all that apply.

options.label: Test failures are visible to the team before the change is merged
It removes the need for code review because the pipeline checks everything a reviewer would
Every change is built and tested in the same clean, repeatable environment
Merged code is guaranteed to be free of bugs once all tests pass
Integration problems between branches are found early, while changes are still small

rubric: Early integration, clean repeatable builds and visible failures are real CI benefits.
Pipelines don't replace review or guarantee bug-free code; passing tests only cover what is tested.

items.prompt: A team builds releases on a developer's laptop and copies them to the server. Twice, a release worked on the laptop but failed in production because a locally installed library version differed. A colleague proposes a pipeline that builds on a fresh agent. Why would this address the problem?

options.label: The pipeline reruns the deployment until it works, which hides any library differences
The agent encrypts the release, which stops library versions from differing in production
A pipeline automatically upgrades every library to the newest version, which makes them all match
A fresh agent installs dependencies from declared files each time, so builds don't depend on one person's machine

rubric: A clean agent builds only from declared dependencies, so results are repeatable.
Distractors suggest encryption, retries or automatic upgrades, none of which fix environment drift.

items.prompt: You want a GitHub Actions workflow to run tests whenever a pull request targets the `main` branch. Which trigger configuration does this?

options.label: `on: { pull_request: { branches: [main] } }`
`on: { push: { tags: [main] } }`
`on: { schedule: { branches: [main] } }`
`on: { workflow_dispatch: { branches: [main] } }`

rubric: The pull_request event with a branches filter runs for PRs targeting main.
Distractors use tags, schedule or manual triggers, which don't fire on pull requests.

items.prompt: You need to order these pipeline steps for a web service: (1) deploy, (2) run tests, (3) check out code, (4) build container image, (5) push image to registry. Which order is correct?
rubric: Check out, test, build, push, then deploy so only tested images are pushed and deployed.
Other orders build before testing, test before checkout, or deploy before the image exists.

items.prompt: In GitHub Actions, a deploy step needs the secret `DEPLOY_TOKEN` stored in repository settings. Which line passes it to the step as an environment variable?

options.label: `env: { DEPLOY_TOKEN: "DEPLOY_TOKEN" }`
`env: { DEPLOY_TOKEN: $(cat .env) }`
`env: { DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ vars.public }} }`
`env: { DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }} }`

rubric: The secrets context reads the stored secret and masks it in logs.
Distractors pass a literal string, a wrong context or a file that would need the secret committed.

items.prompt: Release v42 was deployed from the pipeline, and its health check fails. Artifact v41 is still in the registry and was healthy. What is the quickest safe rollback?

options.label: Revert the commit, then wait for a full rebuild and retest before restoring service
Edit the files on the production server by hand until the check passes
Delete the v42 tag from git so the running service reverts itself
Redeploy the stored v41 artifact through the same deploy job

rubric: Redeploying the known-good artifact restores service fast and uses the normal process.
Distractors are slower, manual or based on the false idea that deleting a tag changes production.

items.prompt: A Node.js pipeline reinstalls all dependencies on every run, taking 4 minutes. You add a cache. Which cache key is best?

options.label: A fixed string like `deps`, so the cache is always reused
A hash of `package-lock.json`, so the cache changes when dependencies change
The current date, so the cache refreshes daily
The commit SHA, so each run gets its own entry

rubric: Keying on the lockfile hash reuses the cache until dependencies change.
A fixed key goes stale, and SHA or date keys rarely produce hits.

items.prompt: You want a `deploy` job to run only after `test` succeeds and only for pushes to `main`. Which GitHub Actions settings help achieve this? Select all that apply.

options.label: `runs-on: main` on the deploy job
`if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` on the deploy job
`continue-on-error: true` on the test job
`needs: test` on the deploy job

rubric: `needs` makes deploy wait for test, and the `if` condition limits it to main.
`continue-on-error` lets failures pass, and `runs-on` selects a runner, not a branch.

items.prompt: A workflow has jobs `test` and `deploy`, with no `needs` setting. A pull request has failing tests, yet the deploy job still ran and shipped the change. The team wants deploy to run only when tests pass. What should you change?

options.label: Add `needs: test` to the deploy job so it waits for a successful test job
Run the workflow twice, so the second run deploys only if the first run passed
Move the deploy commands into the test job's last step and remove the `if` conditions
Set `continue-on-error: true` on the test job so failures are reported separately

rubric: Without `needs`, jobs run in parallel; `needs: test` makes deploy depend on test success.
Other options hide failures, mix concerns or add manual steps instead of declaring the dependency.

items.prompt: A team wants a pipeline that fails as fast and cheaply as possible on a bad commit. Which stage order should they use?

options.label: Deploy to staging, lint, unit tests, build artifact, integration tests
Integration tests, build artifact, lint, unit tests, deploy to production
Lint, unit tests, build artifact, integration tests, deploy to production
Build artifact, deploy to production, unit tests, lint, integration tests

rubric: Cheap, fast checks run first so failures stop the pipeline before costly stages.
Distractors put deployment or slow tests ahead of quick checks, wasting time and risking bad releases.

items.prompt: In GitHub Actions, a deploy job must run only when a commit is pushed to `main`, never for pull request runs. Which condition on the job achieves this?

options.label: `if: github.base_ref == 'main'`
`if: github.actor == 'main'`
`if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'`
`if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'`

rubric: The ref and event name together restrict the job to pushes on main.
`base_ref` is set only on pull requests, so it would select PR runs, and the other options test the wrong fields.

items.prompt: A Node project installs dependencies on every run. You add a dependency cache. Which cache key best ensures the cache is reused until dependencies change?

options.label: The hash of `package-lock.json` combined with the OS name
The commit SHA of the current build
The runner's operating system name only
The current date, so the cache refreshes daily

rubric: Keying on the lockfile hash reuses the cache until dependencies change.
A commit SHA never hits across commits, and the date or OS alone ignores real dependency changes.

items.prompt: A deploy step needs a cloud API token. Which way of supplying it follows safe secrets handling?

options.label: Hardcode it in the workflow YAML as an env value
Store it in the CI secret store and expose it as an env variable to that step
Commit it in a `.env` file in a private repository
Pass it as a command-line argument in the script

rubric: The CI secret store keeps the token out of the repo and limits exposure to the step.
Committed files and YAML persist in history, and command-line args can show in logs and process lists.

items.prompt: Every build is published as an immutable image tagged with its commit SHA. Release `a1b2c3` is faulty and the previous good release was `9f8e7d`. What is the quickest safe rollback?

options.label: Edit the running containers by hand to undo the change
Rebuild the source from `9f8e7d` and deploy the new image
Redeploy the image tagged `9f8e7d` through the deploy step
Revert the commit, wait for the full pipeline, then deploy

rubric: Redeploying the existing tested artifact is fast and deterministic.
Rebuilding or waiting on a full pipeline is slower and may produce a different artifact; manual edits are untracked.

items.prompt: You want builds that give the same result on every run. Which changes help? Select all that apply.

options.label: Install dependencies with `npm ci` from a committed lockfile
Let the build fetch the newest tool versions each run
Pin the base image to a specific version digest
Use the `latest` tag for the build image

rubric: Lockfile installs and pinned images fix inputs so builds repeat.
`latest` and floating tool versions change between runs and break reproducibility.

items.prompt: A pipeline runs sequentially: lint (1 min), unit tests (4 min), integration tests (10 min), end-to-end tests (10 min), total 25 minutes. All four only need the checked-out code and are independent of each other. The team wants the fastest feedback without dropping any check. What should they do?

options.label: Run only the end-to-end tests on every push and the rest nightly
Run the four checks as parallel jobs, gated before the deploy job
Merge lint and unit tests into one stage and keep the rest sequential
Skip integration tests on branches and run them after deploying

rubric: Independent checks in parallel cut wall time to about the longest job, around 10 minutes, and keep every check.
The other options drop or delay checks or save little time.

items.prompt: Integration tests pass when run alone in CI but fail intermittently when four test jobs run in parallel against one shared database. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The jobs overwrite each other's data in the shared database
The lockfile is out of date on only some runners
The unit tests are compiled with a different compiler
The runner's Linux kernel version changes between jobs

rubric: Parallel jobs sharing mutable state interfere, causing intermittent failures.
The other causes would fail consistently or not depend on parallelism.

items.prompt: A pipeline has a `build` job, a `test` job that tests the built artifact, and a `deploy` job that runs the build command again and ships the result. Tests pass, yet production behaves differently. What is the flaw?

options.label: Production needs a larger runner for the build
The test job should run after the deploy job
The deployed binary was rebuilt, so it isn't the artifact that was tested
The deploy job should run fewer build steps to be faster

rubric: Rebuilding at deploy means the shipped output may differ from what was tested; build once and promote.
The other options don't address the mismatch between tested and deployed artifacts.

items.prompt: A secret is masked in CI logs, yet its value appears in a log after a script prints the base64-encoded form of it. Why did masking not prevent this?

options.label: Masking only works on secrets longer than 64 characters
Masking matches the exact stored string, not transformed versions
Masked secrets are shown again when a job is retried
Base64 output is excluded from all log filtering by design

rubric: Masking is exact string matching, so encoded or altered values leak.
The other options invent rules that CI systems don't have.

items.prompt: A workflow uses a trigger that runs on fork pull requests with repository secrets available, and it checks out and runs the PR's code. Which risk does this create?

options.label: Forks will be unable to open pull requests
Untrusted PR code can run with access to secrets and exfiltrate them
The workflow will skip tests for code from forks
Builds will be slower because forks use separate caches

rubric: Running untrusted code with secrets lets a malicious PR steal them.
The other options describe harmless or unrelated effects.

items.prompt: A cache is keyed only by branch name, e.g. `deps-main`. After a developer bumps a library version, CI keeps using the old library and tests pass wrongly. What is the root cause?

options.label: The cache key doesn't change when dependencies change
Tests were run before the cache was saved
The cache is too small to hold the new library
The branch name is too short to be unique

rubric: A key that ignores the lockfile restores stale dependencies after a change.
Size, name length or save timing wouldn't pin an old version.

items.prompt: A rolling deploy shows green and its health check passes, yet users get errors. Which are plausible explanations? Select all that apply.

options.label: The pipeline's lint stage ran before the unit tests
The health check only confirms the process is up, not that it works
A migration made the schema incompatible with instances still on the old version
The deploy job's log used a different timestamp format

rubric: A shallow health check and schema incompatibility during a rolling update both cause errors despite green status.
Stage order of lint and log formats don't affect runtime behaviour.

items.prompt: After release 42 shipped, errors spiked, so the team redeployed the release 41 image. Errors continued: the app now fails with 'column not found'. Release 42 included a migration that dropped a column the old code reads. What best explains why the rollback failed?

options.label: The pipeline cached the release 42 image under the old tag
Release 41's image was corrupted when it was pulled
The rollback ran with an older version of the CI runner
The migration was not backward compatible, so old code can't run on the new schema

rubric: Destructive migrations tie data state to the new code; rollback needs backward-compatible, staged schema changes.
The other causes wouldn't produce a missing-column error.

items.prompt: A pull request's pipeline was green, yet the pipeline on `main` fails right after the merge with a test failure in code the PR never touched. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The main-branch pipeline uses a different programming language version than every other branch
The PR was tested on its own branch without the latest `main`, so the combined result was never run
The PR's tests were skipped entirely because pipelines only execute on the default branch
The merge commit changed the file permissions of the test runner scripts on the build agent

rubric: Testing a branch in isolation misses semantic conflicts with newer changes on the target branch.
Distractors invent environment causes that don't fit a failure in untouched code after a clean merge.

items.prompt: A pipeline caches `node_modules` with the key `deps-${branch_name}`. After a teammate bumps a library in the lockfile, builds on that branch still use the old version and fail oddly. What is the flaw?

options.label: The key never changes when the lockfile changes, so a stale cache keeps being restored
The cache is stored on the runner's disk instead of in a remote registry service
The key includes the branch name, which makes caches unusable across different runners
The cache is too large, so the runner truncates it and drops the newest packages

rubric: Cache keys should include a hash of the lockfile so dependency changes invalidate the cache.
Distractors blame storage location, size or branch naming, none of which explain a stale version.

items.prompt: Integration tests pass when one pipeline run is active but fail about 10% of the time when two runs overlap. Both runs use the same staging database and seed it at test start. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The runner's CPU is throttled when two jobs start, which slows tests past their timeouts
The test framework randomises test order, which breaks tests only when load is high
The database driver caches query plans, which become invalid whenever two clients connect
The runs share mutable state, so one run's seeding or cleanup corrupts the other's data

rubric: Concurrent runs sharing one database interfere; isolate per run with ephemeral databases or schemas.
Distractors offer generic performance or ordering explanations that don't link to overlap of runs.

items.prompt: Staging passed all checks, but production shows a bug that staging never did. The deploy job for each environment runs `npm install && npm run build` from the same commit. What is the most probable underlying problem?

options.label: Each environment builds its own artifact, so unpinned dependencies may resolve differently between builds
Production servers use a faster CPU, so race conditions only appear there
The commit hash changes between the staging and production deploys because Git rewrites history
Staging tests run against a mocked backend, so every real defect is always hidden there

rubric: Building once and promoting the same artifact guarantees what was tested is what ships.
Distractors name plausible environment differences but ignore that the build step itself is repeated.

items.prompt: A pipeline masks the secret `API_KEY` in logs. A debug step runs `echo $API_KEY | base64`, and the encoded key appears readable in the build log. Why did masking fail?

options.label: Masking only applies to jobs on the default branch, so debug steps are always exposed
Masking matches the exact secret string, so a transformed value such as base64 is not recognised
Masking is applied only after the job finishes, so streaming output is never filtered
Masking works only on secrets under 16 characters, so longer keys are printed as-is

rubric: Log masking is a literal string match; encoded or split values bypass it.
Distractors invent timing, branch or length limitations that platforms do not generally impose.

items.prompt: A release containing a database migration is deployed, errors spike, and the team redeploys the previous artifact, but errors continue. Which findings would explain why the rollback did not restore service? Select all that apply.

options.label: The new release changed a shared config value in place that the old version misreads
The migration dropped a column that the previous version still reads
The pipeline's unit tests had passed before the original release
The previous artifact was identical in checksum to the one stored last week
The rollback ran the same deploy script but pulled `latest`, which still points to the new build

rubric: Rollback fails when state, configuration or image references are not reverted along with code.
Passing tests and an unchanged checksum say nothing about why the rollback failed.

items.prompt: An open-source project's workflow runs tests with a `TEST_API_TOKEN` secret. Contributors report that on pull requests from forks, the integration job fails with an authentication error, while PRs from branches in the main repository pass. The workflow file is identical for both. What is the best explanation?

options.label: The token expires after one use, and the first branch PR already consumed it
Forks use a different Git history, so the checkout step fetches an outdated copy of the tests
Fork contributors have lower rate limits on the test API, so the server rejects their requests
Forked PR runs don't receive repository secrets by default, so the token is empty and authentication fails

rubric: Platforms withhold secrets from fork-triggered runs to stop untrusted code from exfiltrating them.
Distractors suggest checkout, token expiry or rate-limit causes that don't depend on fork origin.

items.prompt: Criteria: developers need unit-test feedback within 5 minutes, a 30-minute integration suite is costly, and `main` must stay releasable. Which trigger strategy best meets all three?

options.label: Run unit tests only at release time, and the integration suite on every push for safety
Run every suite on every push to every branch so no defect is missed anywhere
Run unit tests on every push, and the integration suite on PRs before merge via a merge queue
Run all tests only nightly on `main`, and revert any commit that breaks the build

rubric: Fast checks on every push plus the expensive suite as a merge gate balances speed, cost and a releasable main.
Distractors drop either fast feedback, cost control or protection of main.

items.prompt: Criteria: zero downtime, rolling deploys, and the ability to roll back code without data loss. A release must rename a database column. Which approach is best?

options.label: Rename the column manually in production after the pipeline finishes to avoid pipeline failures
Take the service offline briefly, rename the column, then deploy and bring it back
Rename the column in one migration that runs just before the new code starts rolling out
Add the new column, write to both, deploy new code, then drop the old column in a later release

rubric: Expand/contract migrations keep old and new code compatible so rolling deploys and rollbacks stay safe.
Distractors break compatibility during rollout, cause downtime or bypass the pipeline.

items.prompt: Criteria: minimise blast radius if CI is compromised, avoid manual rotation, and keep deploy access to one repository's pipeline. Which credential approach for deploying to a cloud provider is best?

options.label: Commit an encrypted key to the repo and decrypt it with a passphrase stored in CI
Store a long-lived admin key as a CI secret and restrict who can edit the workflow
Use OIDC federation so the job gets short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens bound to that repository
Use the same personal access key as the lead engineer so audits are traceable

rubric: Short-lived federated tokens limit exposure, need no rotation and can be scoped to a repo.
Distractors keep long-lived or over-privileged credentials that increase blast radius.

items.prompt: A team proposes making a flaky end-to-end suite green by auto-retrying each failed test up to three times with no reporting. Judged against the goals of trustworthy signal and fast delivery, what is the best critique?

options.label: It is sound, because any test that passes on a retry proves the code is correct
It is sound, because flaky tests indicate test infrastructure problems that are never worth fixing
It is harmful, because retries always slow pipelines more than the flakiness itself did
It hides real intermittent defects and flakiness trends, so retries should be tracked and flaky tests quarantined and fixed

rubric: Silent retries mask both flaky tests and genuine race conditions; tracking and quarantine preserve signal.
Distractors either accept retries as proof of correctness or overstate their cost.

items.prompt: Criteria: protect against supply-chain tampering of third-party pipeline actions while keeping updates reviewable. Which referencing practice is best for an external action?

options.label: Pin to a major version tag, since maintainers promise never to move it
Reference the default branch to always get the latest security patches instantly
Copy the action's description into the workflow and skip the external code entirely
Pin to a full commit SHA and let an update bot propose reviewed version bumps

rubric: A commit SHA is immutable, and bot PRs keep updates visible and reviewable.
Tags and branches can be moved or hijacked; copying a description doesn't replace the code.

items.prompt: Requirement: every production deployment must be auditable and reproducible months later. Which practices satisfy it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Retain pipeline logs, approvals and deployed artifact versions for the audit period
Define the pipeline and environment config in version control
Deploy only immutable, versioned artifacts built once and traceable to a commit
Redeploy a mutable `latest` tag so the newest build always ships
Let engineers hot-patch servers by SSH when the pipeline is slow

rubric: Immutable traceable artifacts, retained records and versioned config make deployments reproducible and auditable.
Hot patches and mutable tags destroy traceability.

items.prompt: A team can't afford to double its production infrastructure. It wants a bad release to reach at most 5% of users and to revert automatically if the error rate rises. Which release strategy best fits these constraints?

options.label: Canary release sending 5% of traffic to the new version, with automated error-rate checks and rollback
Blue-green with a full duplicate environment and an all-at-once traffic switch
Feature freeze for a month, so each release is tested longer in staging before shipping
Big-bang deploy at night, followed by manual monitoring and a revert if users complain

rubric: Canary limits exposure, needs only a small extra capacity and can auto-rollback on metrics.
Blue-green needs duplicate capacity and switches all users at once; the other options lack limited exposure or automation.

items.prompt: A monorepo has 30 services and a 45-minute full test suite. Criteria: PR feedback in under 10 minutes and no broken main. Which setup best meets both?

options.label: Run affected-service tests on PRs and again on main, with no full run, since dependency graphs are always exact
Run the full suite only nightly and let PRs run lint, since a broken main can be fixed forward the next morning
Run the full suite on every PR using larger runners, since only a complete run can ever protect main from breakage
Run affected-service tests on PRs and the full suite in a merge queue before main is updated

rubric: Affected-only PR runs give fast feedback, and the full run in the merge queue guards main against missed dependencies.
Distractors drop the feedback goal, ignore the time limit, or trust dependency graphs blindly.

items.prompt: A deploy job needs cloud access. Criteria: limit the damage if CI logs or a fork leak a credential, and avoid manual rotation. Which approach is best?

options.label: Put a personal access key for each developer on the shared runner image so any leak can be traced to one person
Federate the runner identity through OIDC to a role limited to this repo and branch, issuing short-lived tokens per run
Store a long-lived deploy key as a masked repository secret and rotate it every quarter using a calendar reminder
Commit an encrypted key file to the repo and keep its decryption passphrase in a masked CI variable for safety

rubric: OIDC federation gives short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials with no rotation to manage.
Static keys, even masked or encrypted, stay valid after a leak, and keys baked into runner images widen exposure.

items.prompt: A pipeline runs `docker build` separately in its staging job and its prod job from the same commit. Which critique of this design is strongest?

options.label: What passed staging is not necessarily what ships, since base-image or dependency drift can change the prod build; build once, promote by digest
Prod images should be built on a release engineer's laptop so that they can inspect the result before it is shipped
Building in each job is fine because the same commit guarantees identical output, so only job ordering matters here
The two builds double compute cost, which is the main flaw, and layer caching would resolve the whole problem

rubric: Testing one artifact and shipping another breaks the guarantee that staging validated what runs in prod.
Distractors treat the issue as cost, assume a commit determines build output, or add a manual, unreproducible step.

items.prompt: A test fails intermittently and blocks unrelated PRs. Criteria: keep main trustworthy, keep the signal, and avoid permanent debt. Which handling is best?

options.label: Move it to a non-blocking job that still runs and reports, with a named owner and a deadline to fix or remove it
Delete the test now, because an intermittently failing test gives no information and costs every reviewer time
Retry every failing test three times and report success if any attempt passes, so intermittent failures never block merges
Mark the whole suite non-blocking until flakiness is gone, since blocking on any test punishes unrelated authors

rubric: Quarantine with ownership and a deadline preserves the signal and bounds the debt without blocking others.
Blanket retries hide real failures, and deleting or unblocking everything loses coverage.

items.prompt: A release drops a column that the previous app version still reads. Criteria: zero downtime and the ability to roll back the app within an hour. Which plan is best?

options.label: Ship code that stops using the column first, then drop it in a later release once rollback is no longer needed
Run the drop migration first in a pre-deploy job, since old instances will retry failed queries until they update
Deploy the migration and new app together in one step; rollback means redeploying the old app image only
Take a maintenance window, drop the column, and restore from backup if the app needs to be rolled back

rubric: Expand/contract keeps old and new app versions compatible with the schema, so rollback and zero downtime both hold.
Other options break the old version, add downtime, or rely on retries that cannot succeed.

items.prompt: A workflow triggered by `pull_request_target` checks out the PR head from forks and runs `npm test` with repository secrets and a write-scoped token available. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Untrusted fork code runs beside secrets and a write token, so a malicious test script can exfiltrate them
PR code should never be tested at all, since only code already merged to main is safe to execute
Run untrusted code in a no-secrets `pull_request` workflow and keep privileged steps in a separate workflow that uses only trusted inputs
Limit the token to read-only permissions and require approval before workflows run for first-time contributors
Masking secrets in logs is sufficient, because code that runs in the job cannot reveal a masked value elsewhere

rubric: The risk is untrusted code running with privileges; the fixes are separation, least privilege and approval gates.
Masking only hides log output, and refusing to test PRs defeats CI.

items.prompt: A payments service runs on 20 pods. A new version changes retry logic, and bugs would show only under real traffic. A bad version can create duplicate charges that cannot be reversed. Criteria: limit customers exposed and detect problems fast. Which release strategy is best?

options.label: Rolling update in batches of five pods, relying on readiness probes to catch any faulty behaviour before it spreads
Canary to a small share of traffic with automated checks on duplicate-charge and error metrics, halting promotion on breach
Blue-green swap of all traffic at once, since an instant switch back makes the amount of exposure irrelevant
Release to staging with synthetic traffic, then to everyone, since staging reproduces production load patterns accurately

rubric: A metric-gated canary caps exposure, which matters because the harm cannot be undone by switching back.
Blue-green and rolling updates expose many customers, and readiness probes or staging cannot reveal logic bugs found only in real traffic.

items.prompt: Design requirements: the same bytes must run in dev, staging and prod; prod needs manual approval; configuration differs per environment. Which pipeline design meets all of them?

options.label: Build in dev, then copy source to staging and prod, where the same Dockerfile rebuilds it to keep the images consistent
Each environment job rebuilds from the release tag with an environment-specific build argument, and prod waits for approval
Build once, record the image digest, deploy that digest to every environment with config injected at deploy time, prod gated
Build once and bake production config into the image, then override files inside running dev containers by hand

rubric: Build-once, promote-by-digest with deploy-time config satisfies identical bytes, per-environment config and the prod gate.
Rebuilding or baking config produces different artifacts, and manual edits break reproducibility.

items.prompt: Design a dependency cache for a Node CI job. Constraints: never restore dependencies that disagree with the lockfile, work across OS runners, and reuse across branches. Which design fits?

options.label: Key on the commit SHA so the cache is always exact, caching node_modules and restoring from the previous commit's key
Key on runner OS plus a lockfile hash, cache the content-addressed package store, and run the lockfile install every time
Use one fixed key such as `deps-v1` for all OSes and branches, caching node_modules and bumping the version manually
Key on branch name so each branch has its own cache, caching node_modules and skipping install whenever the cache hits

rubric: Keying on OS and lockfile hash allows cross-branch reuse, and the install step guarantees agreement with the lockfile.
Branch, SHA or fixed keys either prevent reuse or restore mismatched or OS-specific modules.

items.prompt: Merge A then merge B trigger deploys, but A's deploy finishes after B's and overwrites it with the older version. Constraints: every commit still gets tested, an older version must never end up live, and a running deploy must not be cancelled mid-way. Which fix meets all of them?

options.label: Cancel any in-progress deploy when a newer run starts, so the newest commit always wins the race for the environment
Add a ten-minute sleep before each deploy so earlier commits have time to finish before later ones begin deploying
Skip tests on deploy runs so each finishes faster, making out-of-order completion unlikely in normal operation
Serialize deploys in one concurrency group without cancelling the running one, and skip a queued deploy if a newer commit is already live

rubric: Serialized deploys without cancellation plus a staleness check prevent regressions and half-applied deploys.
Cancelling mid-way violates a constraint, and sleeps or skipped tests do not remove the race.

items.prompt: Design requirements: revert within 5 minutes of an SLO breach after release, lose no data, and ship schema changes separately and compatibly. Which design meets them?

options.label: Compare errors with yesterday in a nightly job that pages on-call, who restore the last database backup and the old image
Run a post-deploy smoke test that checks the home page returns 200 and reverts migrations with a down script on failure
Gradual rollout with automated error-rate and latency checks that redeploy the previous digest on breach, with backward-compatible migrations
Keep the old version on standby and have developers flip traffic by hand after they notice alerts in the team chat

rubric: Automated SLO-driven rollback to the prior digest meets the time limit, and compatible migrations avoid data loss.
Other options are too slow, too shallow, or rely on destructive restores and manual action.

items.prompt: A pipeline runs PR tests, builds an image, pushes it to a registry and deploys on merge using OIDC credentials. A new requirement says auditors must be able to verify that only unmodified, CI-built images run in prod. What is the design missing?

options.label: Longer log retention for CI runs so that auditors can read the full build output for each release
A second human approval before the push to the registry, so that every image stored there has been reviewed
A vulnerability scan that fails builds when base images carry high-severity findings before they are pushed
Image signing or provenance attestation in CI, with the cluster verifying it before admitting any image

rubric: Signed or attested artifacts verified at admission prove origin and integrity, which is what the requirement demands.
Approvals, logs and scans help other goals but do not prove that the running image is the CI-built one.

items.prompt: Design a hotfix path with these constraints: ship within 30 minutes, never bypass required checks, and keep an audit trail. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Deploy from the engineer's laptop with a break-glass key and write up the audit trail after the incident
An admin-only flag that skips tests and merges the fix straight to main when an incident is declared
Reuse the standard promote-by-digest deploy, with a named approver and a linked incident ticket recorded
Branch from the released tag, run the same pipeline with the same required checks, and parallelise its stages
Reserved warm runners and cache so that queue time does not consume the 30-minute budget

rubric: Speed comes from parallelism and reserved capacity, while the checks, artifact flow and approval record stay intact.
Skip flags and laptop deploys bypass checks or weaken the audit trail.

items.prompt: A service runs in three regions with compatible schemas. Requirements: a bad release reaches at most one region before detection, all regions end on the same version within a day, and no manual per-region steps. Which pipeline design meets all of them?

options.label: Deploy all three regions in parallel from one job and roll all of them back if any health check fails
Deploy the first region automatically, then let each regional team trigger its own deployment when it is ready
Deploy region by region in waves with a bake time and automated health gate, halting and reverting the affected region on failure
Deploy only to the lowest-traffic region and leave the others on the old version until the next scheduled release

rubric: Automated waves with health gates limit blast radius, converge on one version and need no manual steps.
Parallel deploys expose every region, manual triggers break automation, and a single-region release violates convergence.
